Global mutual fund activity strengthened in 2024 as both market valuations and investor appetite improved alongside moderating inflation, interest rate cuts in major economies, resilient corporate earnings, particularly in technology and AI-linked sectors, and generally stronger economic sentiment. The decision by the US Federal Reserve to lower rates in September 2024 signalled a shift in monetary policy and this affected the cost of borrowing, investors decision and currency valuations. Solid economic growth and a decrease in inflation rates around the world provided a recipe for investors to make bold decisions as the value of stocks and bonds increased. These dynamics lifted asset prices across equities, bonds, and money markets, contributing to a 7.10% rise in global mutual fund ending NAV as reported by the Investment Company Institute (ICI). Equity funds expanded the most, with NAV increasing 12.26% to US$35.7 trillion, while bond funds grew 6.98% to US$13.8 trillion as investors positioned ahead of anticipated rate reductions. Money-market funds also posted double-digit growth of 11.54% to US$11.6 trillion1, reflecting continued demand for liquidity in an uncertain environment.

Against this global backdrop, the Cayman Islands fund sector continued to expand, supported by these same valuation effects and by sustained international demand for Cayman-domiciled structures. The number of regulated funds increased from 29,353 in 2023 to 30,150 in 2024 (up 2.72%), driven largely by growth in Registered and Private Funds, even as Master, Administered, Licensed and Limited Investor Funds saw marginal declines. Filing compliance remained strong, with an 83.18% Fund Annual Return (FAR) submission rate, comparable to the previous year. Reflecting strong global market performance, Cayman funds submitting a FAR reported aggregate ending NAV of US$9.194 trillion, a 9.88% increase relative to 2023—outpacing the global growth rate. This demonstrates the close integration and responsiveness of Cayman’s fund sector to global asset-price movements and investor flows.

Worldwide, regulated open-end funds increased from 140, 908 (revised) in 2023 to 143,858 at the end of 2024, with aggregate NAV of US$73.9 trillion (up from US$69.0 trillion), with strong inflows into equity and bond funds contributing to this expansion. Equity funds account for 48.31% of total ending NAV of worldwide funds followed by bonds at 18.67%; money market funds at 15.70% with the remaining 17.32% consisting of Other/Balanced/Mixed.2 Europe leads with the largest number of funds at 42%, Asia-Pacific at 29%, Rest of the World 22% and United States at 7% although total ending NAV for US funds accounts for 53% of ending NAV compared to Europe at 31%, Asia-Pacific at 11% and Rest of the World at 5%. As at year end 2024, assets held by mutual funds accounted for 26.67% of worldwide capital markets of US$277.1 trillion as measured by the value of equity and debt securities outstanding. The remaining 73.33% were held by a wide range of other investors, such as central banks, sovereign wealth funds, pension plans (both defined benefit and defined contribution), banks, insurance companies, hedge funds and private equity funds, broker-dealers, and households’ direct holdings of stocks and bonds. 3

These trends were mirrored within the Cayman Islands, where net inflows reached US$682 billion, consistent with global mutual-fund net sales of US$2.3 trillion. Cayman funds benefited from robust investor reinvestment behaviour observed internationally - particularly in the US, where US mutual fund shareholders reinvested over US$1.1 trillion in dividends and capital-gains distributions. The continuing shift toward lower-cost and more flexible investment vehicles was evident globally, with Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) registering over US$1.1 trillion in net share issuance in 2024. Deloitte predicts that assets under administration for active ETFs in the US will grow from US$856 billion to US$11 trillion by the end of 2035 but there will be a compound annual decline of 4% for mutual funds during this period.4 While this shift has created competitive pressures for traditional mutual funds, Cayman continues to attract a large share of both structures given its established role in cross-border fund formation.

Global mutual fund flows strengthened in 2024, with equity funds receiving US$909 billion in net inflows and bond funds attracting US$1.4 trillion—more than double the previous year. Anticipated interest rate cuts boosted demand for bonds, as investors sought to lock in higher yields before prices rose. Performance varied across sectors, with funds exposed to technology, financial services, and emerging markets outperforming, while many actively managed large-cap U.S. equity funds lagged the S&P 500. Overall demand was shaped by shifting interest-rate expectations, macroeconomic uncertainty, demographic trends, and the continued preference for low-cost indexed products.

Cayman-domiciled funds also recorded stronger financial performance in 2024. Aggregate net income rose 43.57% to US$926 billion, dividends nearly doubled to US$769 billion, and performance fees increased by 30% from US$40 billion in 2023 to US$52 billion in 2024. Returns on both net and gross assets improved, reflecting higher net income, rising global asset prices and continued investor confidence. The Investment Company Industry research has classified 842 mutual funds and ETFs with assets of US$570 billion as investing in exclusionary, inclusionary, or impact investing ESG criteria, and although the net assets increased in 2024, the number of funds decreased likely due to weaker demand for these funds over the past two years. In fact, net outflows from ESG-criteria funds were US$8 billion in 2023 and US$13 billion in 2024.5 These subdued trends in ESG-type funds were also mirrored within the Cayman context as total ending NAV of investments classified as Activism & ESG fell to US$59 billion in 2024 compared to US$71 billion in 2023.

The Cayman Islands continues to be a preferred jurisdiction for fund administration, particularly in NAV calculation and registrar/transfer-agent services. According to the 2025 Investments Factbook, there were 787 fund sponsors from around the world competing in the US market to provide investments managers services. Nevertheless, Cayman remains a leading domicile for fund structures managed by US-based investment managers, with 9,934 funds (NAV US$5.086 trillion) managed from the US (Delaware and New York as the most popular destinations). Additional activity came from investment managers located in Cayman (1,822 funds), the UK (1,014 funds), and other global financial centres, underscoring the jurisdiction’s continued integration with international capital markets.

Based on 2024 submissions, the Cayman Islands and the United States continue to remain the two largest sources of investors for Cayman-domiciled funds, with both jurisdictions maintaining investor counts of over 6,000. Noteworthy, is that while the Cayman Islands saw a slight decline in the number of investors, the value of net assets held by Cayman-based investors increased materially, rising from US$2.07 trillion to US$2.25 trillion in 2024. Several other major jurisdictions e.g., Japan, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Luxembourg and Ireland, also retained top 10 ranking, with modest year-on-year shifts in number of investors and net assets. Across the year, most of the top 10 countries experienced an increase in the value of net assets invested, likely driven not just by additional capital allocated but also favourable market conditions and improved fund performances in 2024. Overall, the trend points to both market appreciation and sustained confidence in Cayman as a preferred jurisdiction for fund structuring.

Overall, 2024 underscored the close alignment between global financial conditions and the performance of Cayman’s fund sector. The favourable global macroeconomic environment, combined with strong investor participation and rising asset valuations, translated into higher NAVs, net inflows, and stronger operational results for Cayman-domiciled funds. This reinforces the jurisdiction’s central role in global investment intermediation while highlighting the importance of continued vigilance as global conditions evolve.

In 2024, global financial conditions improved, and inflation continued to ease. After several years of interest rate hikes to combat inflation, the world economies moved towards a soft landing. The US and Asia-Pacific stock market grew by approximately 24% and 10%, respectively. This contributed to stronger mutual funds’ performance, as evidenced by higher net income, dividends, and closing NAV at the end of 2024.

Global economic growth was 3.3% in 2024. This was primarily driven by resilient service sectors and moderating inflation, particularly in advanced economies. However, emerging markets and developing economies showed a slight slowdown from their 2023 pace. Furthermore, escalating trade tensions, geopolitical conflicts, and policy uncertainty remained. In 2025, the US tariffs and increased uncertainty negatively impacted business sentiment and disrupted supply chains, and these developments may affect the projected economic growth rates of 3.2% and 3.1% in 2026.

The US economy grew by 2.8% in 2024, outperforming many other developed countries, supported by a healthy labour market, resilient consumer spending driven by front-loaded demand ahead of tariff hikes, and robust domestic investment. However, real GDP growth is expected to fall to 1.5% in 2025 and 1.3% in 2026 due to the impact of higher tariffs, subdued private sector sentiment, higher inflation, softening labour market conditions, margin pressures, reduced business investment and weakening consumer demand.6 Unemployment in July 2024 was 4.2% and remained stable for the rest of the year. Additionally, Inflation declined from 3.4% in December 2023 to 2.4% in September 2024 before rebounding to 2.9% at year-end. With declining inflation and cooling economic activity, the FED cut interest rates three times in the second half of 2024, starting in September, and by year-end rates had fallen by 100 basis points. Strong corporate earnings, easing inflation, and the FED’s interest rate cuts fuelled equity market gain. Bonds performed well in the first three quarters of 2024 with a total return of 5.2% through September. In the last quarter, however, bond markets reversed course, and the year ended with a total return of 1.8%.7

In China, real GDP grew by 5.0% in 2024 and this was primarily driven by exports, manufacturing, and investments. However, domestic consumption slowed in 2024 after playing a central role in driving growth in 2023. Real GDP is projected to grow by 4.0% through 2026 but key risks remain, including ongoing vulnerabilities in the real estate sector, fiscal pressures, and deflationary trends in consumer behaviour as well as renewed pressures from trade tensions and US tariffs.

In the Euro Area, economic growth was approximately 0.9%, supported by public spending, particularly defence expenditure in Germany, and a gradual recovery of private consumption. This occurred despite challenges such as tariffs, geopolitical risks and weaknesses in the manufacturing sector that weighed on exports and investment. Economic growth in 2025 is expected to ease to 0.8%, with a modest improvement to 1.6% projected in 2026.

Global headline inflation, driven by supply-side factors such as pandemic-era supply chain disruptions, labour force distortions, and the repercussions of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, was reported at 5.7% in 2024. However, it is projected to decline to 4.3% in 2025 and 3.6% in 2026, supported by easing commodity prices. Nonetheless, cost pressures persist due to emerging trade frictions and structural challenges, and the fight against inflation will continue to dominate the global economic policy agenda in the short to medium term.

Finally, artificial intelligence (AI) now plays an important role in the mutual fund industry by assisting in human decision making, automating operations, and providing data-driven insights. AI enhances stock-picking capabilities, reduces transaction costs and is less prone to behavioural biases. However, due to ethical and regulatory considerations, AI is expected to complement rather than replace human expertise.
